reg-kalmar-union.why: Margaret I already ruled Denmark and Norway, and Swedish nobles invited her in after turning against their king, Albert of Mecklenburg, whom her forces defeated in 1389. A single crown also promised a stronger hand against the German Hanseatic League, which dominated Baltic trade.
reg-kalmar-union.impact: Each kingdom kept its own laws and council, but power drifted towards Denmark, and Swedish resentment over taxes and wars produced repeated revolts. After Sweden left, Denmark and Norway stayed joined until 1814, shaping the borders and rivalries of modern Scandinavia.

reg-granada-falls.why: The marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile joined Spain's two largest Christian kingdoms and gave them the resources for a ten-year campaign. Granada, long a tribute-paying survivor, was weakened by a dynastic feud inside its ruling Nasrid family.
reg-granada-falls.impact: The surrender terms promised Muslims freedom of worship, but forced conversions followed within a decade, and the descendants of converts, the Moriscos, were expelled in the early 1600s. Victory strengthened the crown's drive for religious uniformity and freed attention and money for overseas ventures.

reg-st-petersburg.why: Peter had toured western Europe and wanted a navy and direct sea trade, but Russia's only real port, Arkhangelsk, was frozen for much of the year. The Great Northern War against Sweden, begun in 1700, gave him the chance to seize the mouth of the Neva.
reg-st-petersburg.impact: The new city became home to Russia's Baltic fleet, court and academies, and nobles were ordered to build houses there. It pulled Russian government and culture towards Europe, and later became the stage for the revolutions of 1905 and 1917.

reg-italy-unified.why: Since 1815 the peninsula had been split among several states, with Austria dominant in the north. Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, won French help for a war against Austria in 1859, which gave Piedmont Lombardy and set off risings in the central duchies.
reg-italy-unified.impact: The new state took Piedmont's constitution, king and centralised administration, which many southerners experienced as conquest, and a lasting economic gap between north and south followed. The seizure of papal territory began a quarrel with the Catholic Church that was not settled until the Lateran Treaty of 1929.

reg-easter-rising.why: Home Rule for Ireland had been passed in 1914 but suspended for the war, and the secret Irish Republican Brotherhood saw Britain's difficulty as an opportunity. Its military council planned the rising using the Irish Volunteers and James Connolly's smaller Irish Citizen Army.
reg-easter-rising.impact: Support swung from the moderate Home Rule party to Sinn Féin, which won most Irish seats in the 1918 election and set up its own parliament in Dublin. A guerrilla war followed, ending in the 1921 treaty that created the Irish Free State and confirmed the island's partition.

reg-velvet-revolution.why: Czechoslovakia had been under hard-line rule since Soviet-led forces crushed the Prague Spring in 1968. By autumn 1989 Gorbachev had made clear that Moscow would not intervene, Poland and Hungary were already reforming, and the Berlin Wall had opened eight days before the march.
reg-velvet-revolution.impact: Free elections followed in June 1990, the first since 1946, and Soviet troops left the country in 1991. Disagreements between Czech and Slovak leaders over the federation and the pace of economic reform led to a peaceful split into two states on 1 January 1993.

reg-forbidden-city.why: The Yongle Emperor had seized the throne from his nephew in a civil war, and his power base lay in the north at Beijing, not in the existing capital, Nanjing. A northern capital also put the court closer to the Mongol frontier, where he campaigned in person.
reg-forbidden-city.impact: Beijing has remained China's capital for most of the centuries since, and the palace's north-south axis still fixes the layout of the city centre. After the last emperor was expelled in 1924, the complex opened to the public as the Palace Museum the following year.

reg-tokugawa-shogunate.why: Japan had been torn by more than a century of warfare between rival lords. Oda Nobunaga and then Toyotomi Hideyoshi had largely reunified it, and when Hideyoshi died in 1598 leaving a child heir, Ieyasu, the most powerful of the regents, moved to take control.
reg-tokugawa-shogunate.impact: The shogunate controlled the regional lords by requiring them to spend alternate years in Edo, and from the 1630s it banned Christianity and restricted foreign trade to a few ports. Long peace brought growing cities, commerce and popular arts such as kabuki and woodblock prints.

reg-singapore-founded.why: The Dutch controlled most ports on the sea route between India and China, and the British East India Company wanted a base of its own near the Strait of Malacca. Raffles exploited a succession dispute in the Johor sultanate, recognising the claimant who was willing to sign.
reg-singapore-founded.impact: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 confirmed British possession, and Singapore became part of the Straits Settlements and later a major naval base. Migration, largely from southern China, India and the Malay world, created the mixed population of the independent city-state that emerged in 1965.

reg-hong-kong-handover.why: Hong Kong Island and Kowloon had been ceded outright after the Opium Wars, but the much larger New Territories were held on a 99-year lease from 1898. As its expiry neared, Britain and China negotiated, and their 1984 Joint Declaration agreed the return of the whole territory.
reg-hong-kong-handover.impact: Hong Kong kept its own currency, courts and border, and remained a major financial centre. Disputes over how its leaders are chosen led to large protests in 2014 and 2019, and a national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020 sharply narrowed the space for political opposition.

reg-berlin-conference.why: Rival claims in the Congo basin by Leopold II, France and Portugal threatened to cause conflict between European powers. Steamships, quinine and modern firearms had made the African interior accessible, and governments wanted agreed rules for trade and for claiming territory.
reg-berlin-conference.impact: The principle that claims required effective occupation hastened the dispatch of troops and officials inland. Borders were later drawn with little regard for existing peoples and states, and many survive as national frontiers today. Leopold's Congo Free State became notorious for forced labour and mass deaths.

reg-adwa.why: Italy, already holding Eritrea, claimed that the 1889 Treaty of Wuchale made Ethiopia its protectorate. The Italian and Amharic texts differed on this point, and Menelik rejected the Italian reading. He had spent years importing modern rifles and artillery, and regional rulers rallied to him.
reg-adwa.impact: The Italian government of Francesco Crispi fell within days, and the Treaty of Addis Ababa cancelled the protectorate claim. Ethiopia stayed independent through the colonial era except for the Italian occupation of 1936 to 1941, which Mussolini presented partly as revenge for Adwa.

reg-algeria-independence.why: Algeria was governed as part of France itself, but its Muslim majority had few political rights while European settlers held the best land. After hopes of reform faded and protests were bloodily suppressed at Sétif in 1945, the FLN launched an armed uprising in November 1954.
reg-algeria-independence.impact: Charles de Gaulle, returned to power by the crisis, negotiated the Évian Accords that ended the fighting. The FLN went on to rule Algeria as a one-party state for decades. In France, the use of torture and the fate of Algerians who had fought for France remained painful subjects.

reg-south-africa-1994.why: Internal resistance, international sanctions and a stagnating economy had made apartheid increasingly hard to sustain. In 1990 President F. W. de Klerk lifted the ban on the ANC and released Nelson Mandela after 27 years in prison, opening several years of tense negotiations.
reg-south-africa-1994.impact: A government of national unity took office, and a new constitution with a strong bill of rights followed in 1996. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission heard testimony on apartheid-era abuses. Political equality was achieved, though deep economic inequality between racial groups has persisted.

reg-mayflower.why: Many of the passengers were English Separatists who had broken with the Church of England and lived for some years in Leiden in the Dutch Republic. Worried about poverty and about their children losing their English identity, they obtained backing from London investors to settle in America.
reg-mayflower.impact: Plymouth survived with help from the Wampanoag, whose leader Massasoit made a treaty with the settlers in 1621. The colony stayed small and was absorbed into Massachusetts in 1691, but its story, including the 1621 harvest feast, became central to American national tradition.

reg-haiti-independence.why: French Saint-Domingue was the richest sugar colony in the Caribbean, worked by roughly half a million enslaved Africans under brutal conditions. The French Revolution divided the colony's free population and spread talk of rights, and in 1791 the enslaved rose in the north.
reg-haiti-independence.impact: The loss helped persuade Napoleon to sell Louisiana to the United States in 1803. Slaveholding powers shunned the new state, and in 1825 France demanded a large indemnity in return for recognition, a debt that burdened Haiti for generations. The revolution inspired enslaved people and abolitionists elsewhere.

reg-mexico-independence.why: Earlier risings under the priests Hidalgo and Morelos had been defeated. In 1820 a liberal revolution in Spain alarmed conservative Mexican elites, and the royalist officer Iturbide changed sides, agreeing with the rebel Vicente Guerrero on a plan promising independence, the Catholic religion and unity between Mexicans and Spaniards.
reg-mexico-independence.impact: Iturbide was crowned emperor in 1822 but was overthrown within a year, and Mexico became a republic in 1824. Decades of instability followed, with frequent changes of government, the loss of Texas, and the cession of vast northern territories to the United States in 1848.

reg-canada-confederation.why: Political deadlock between English and French speakers in the united Province of Canada pushed leaders to seek a wider federation. The American Civil War raised fears of invasion from the United States, and Britain wanted its colonies to carry more of their own defence costs.
reg-canada-confederation.impact: The federal system gave provinces control of matters such as education, which helped protect French language and civil law in Quebec. The dominion bought the Hudson's Bay Company's lands in 1870 and built a transcontinental railway, expanding west at heavy cost to Indigenous and Métis peoples.

reg-cuban-revolution.why: Fulgencio Batista had taken power in a 1952 coup, cancelling elections, and his rule was marked by corruption and repression. Castro's failed attack on the Moncada barracks in 1953 gave his movement its name. By 1958 army morale had collapsed and Washington had halted arms shipments.
reg-cuban-revolution.impact: The new government nationalised land and foreign-owned businesses, and the United States responded with a trade embargo that largely remains in place. Many middle-class Cubans emigrated to Florida. Castro led a one-party socialist state until 2008, and the revolution encouraged guerrilla movements across Latin America.

reg-atahualpa-captured.why: Atahualpa had just defeated his half-brother Huáscar in a civil war over the succession, which followed an epidemic, probably smallpox, that killed the previous emperor. Confident in the large army camped nearby, he agreed to meet the small Spanish party in the town square.
reg-atahualpa-captured.impact: The Spanish marched on Cusco, ruling at first through puppet emperors, and founded Lima in 1535. An Inca remnant held out at Vilcabamba until 1572. Andean silver, above all from Potosí, went on to finance the Spanish empire, while disease and forced labour devastated the population.

reg-argentina-independence.why: Buenos Aires had governed itself since 1810 in the name of the captive Spanish king, Ferdinand VII. His restoration in 1814 and his attempt to recover the colonies by force ended that pretence, and San Martín pressed the delegates for a clear declaration.
reg-argentina-independence.impact: The declaration did not settle how the country would be governed. Decades of conflict followed between those favouring a dominant Buenos Aires and provincial federalists, while Paraguay, Bolivia and Uruguay went their own ways. A lasting national constitution came only in 1853.

reg-ayacucho.why: Peru was the stronghold of Spanish power in South America, and San Martín's 1821 declaration of independence there had not dislodged the royalist army in the highlands. Bolívar arrived from the north in 1823 and won at Junín in August 1824, forcing a final battle.
reg-ayacucho.impact: Upper Peru became independent the following year as Bolivia, named after Bolívar, with Sucre as an early president. The last Spanish garrison, at Callao, held out until 1826. Bolívar's hope of a wider union failed, and the former colonies became separate republics.

reg-brasilia.why: Moving the capital inland had been written into Brazil's first republican constitution in 1891, to draw people and investment away from the crowded coast. Little was done until Kubitschek made it the centrepiece of his 1955 election campaign and his development programme.
reg-brasilia.impact: New highways linked the interior to the coast and encouraged settlement of the centre-west. The cost added to inflation and public debt. Planned for about half a million people, the capital region now holds several million, many in satellite towns outside Costa's original plan.

reg-tasman-new-zealand.why: The Dutch East India Company, based at Batavia, sent Tasman to look for a rumoured rich southern continent and a sea route across the Pacific to Chile. Weeks earlier on the same voyage he had reached the island now called Tasmania.
reg-tasman-new-zealand.impact: Dutch mapmakers soon renamed the land Nova Zeelandia, after the province of Zeeland, giving the country its name. The company saw no profit in it and did not follow up, so Māori society continued without European contact until James Cook charted the coasts in 1769.

reg-first-fleet.why: Britain had shipped convicts to its American colonies until the War of Independence closed that outlet, leaving prisons and prison hulks overcrowded. Botany Bay, reported on favourably by Joseph Banks after Cook's 1770 voyage, was chosen in 1786 as a new destination.
reg-first-fleet.impact: The colony came close to starvation in its first years before farming took hold. About 160,000 convicts were transported to Australia before the practice ended in 1868. For the Aboriginal peoples of the Sydney region, settlement brought loss of land, violence and a devastating epidemic in 1789.

reg-eureka-stockade.why: The gold rush that began in Victoria in 1851 drew tens of thousands of diggers, who had to buy a costly licence whether or not they found gold and had no vote. Heavy-handed police licence hunts and the acquittal of a hotel owner suspected of killing a miner brought matters to a head.
reg-eureka-stockade.impact: A cheaper miner's right replaced the licence and carried the right to vote, and Lalor himself was elected to Victoria's parliament. The rebellion is often described as the birthplace of Australian democracy, though historians differ on how much it really changed.

reg-nz-suffrage.why: The campaign grew out of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which wanted women's votes to help restrict alcohol. Several bills narrowly failed from 1887 onwards. In 1893 the liquor trade lobbied hard against the measure, but it passed the upper house by two votes.
reg-nz-suffrage.impact: Māori women gained the vote at the same time. Women could not stand for parliament until 1919, and the first was elected in 1933. The result encouraged suffrage campaigners in Australia, Britain and the United States, who pointed to New Zealand as proof that it worked.

reg-png-independence.why: Australia administered Papua from 1906 and the former German New Guinea after the First World War, later under United Nations trusteeship. From the 1960s the UN pressed for decolonisation, an elected assembly was created, and Gough Whitlam's government moved quickly, granting self-government in 1973.
reg-png-independence.impact: The country kept a parliamentary system and close aid and trade ties with Australia. Holding together so many distinct communities proved difficult, most seriously on Bougainville, where a secessionist conflict from 1988 to 1998 cost many lives and led to an autonomy agreement.

spc-laika.why: After Sputnik 1's success, Khrushchev wanted a second spectacular in time for the fortieth anniversary of the October Revolution on 7 November. Engineers had only about four weeks, too little to design a recovery system. Soviet teams had already flown dogs on short suborbital rocket flights.
spc-laika.impact: The flight added to American alarm about Soviet rocket power. Later Soviet dog flights were designed to return, and Belka and Strelka came back alive in 1960, clearing the way for Gagarin. The true cause of Laika's death was only made public in 2002.

spc-nasa-founded.why: Sputnik in October 1957 shocked American opinion, and the navy's Vanguard rocket exploded on live television that December. Rival army, navy and air force programmes were duplicating effort, and Eisenhower preferred a civilian agency that would keep space science separate from the military.
spc-nasa-founded.impact: NASA took over the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and later Wernher von Braun's army rocket team, and started the Mercury programme within days of opening. Its budget peaked in the mid-1960s during Apollo. It remains the world's best-funded space agency, running planetary probes, telescopes and crewed flights.

spc-luna-2.why: The Soviet R-7 rocket, fitted with an upper stage, was powerful enough to send a probe to the Moon. Several earlier attempts had failed at launch, and Luna 1 missed the Moon in January 1959. The September flight came just before Khrushchev's visit to the United States.
spc-luna-2.impact: Its instruments found no significant magnetic field around the Moon and confirmed the stream of charged particles from the Sun now called the solar wind. A month later Luna 3 photographed the far side for the first time. The successes deepened American fears of falling behind in rocketry.

spc-shepard.why: Project Mercury had chosen seven military test pilots in 1959. Shepard's flight might have come in March 1961, but Wernher von Braun insisted on one more unmanned test of the Redstone rocket, which was too weak to reach orbit. Gagarin flew on 12 April.
spc-shepard.impact: Unlike Soviet flights, the launch was broadcast live, and its success restored some American confidence after Gagarin and the Bay of Pigs failure. John Glenn made the first American orbital flight in February 1962. Shepard later commanded Apollo 14 and walked on the Moon in 1971.

spc-tereshkova.why: Soviet officials, aware that American women pilots had passed astronaut medical tests, wanted another first. Five women were selected in 1962, chosen mainly from parachutists because Vostok cosmonauts ejected before landing. Tereshkova's working-class background also suited Soviet publicity.
spc-tereshkova.impact: She became an international symbol for the Soviet Union and later a politician. The women's group was disbanded without any of the others flying, and the next woman in space, Svetlana Savitskaya, did not fly until 1982. The first American woman followed in 1983.

spc-leonov-spacewalk.why: The Soviet programme knew that NASA planned a spacewalk during its Gemini flights and wanted to get there first. The Voskhod was a modified Vostok capsule, and engineers added an inflatable airlock so that the cabin did not have to be emptied of air.
spc-leonov-spacewalk.impact: Ed White made the first American spacewalk less than three months later. Leonov's difficulties were kept from the public for years. The experience showed that suits must stay flexible under pressure, and working outside a spacecraft later became routine for building and repairing space stations.

spc-apollo-8.why: The mission was planned as an Earth-orbit test, but the lunar module was not ready. NASA managers, aware of intelligence suggesting the Soviets might send cosmonauts around the Moon, decided in August 1968 to send the command module to lunar orbit instead.
spc-apollo-8.impact: The flight proved the navigation, communications and engine burns needed to reach the Moon and return, making a landing in 1969 realistic. The Soviet Union never flew its crewed circumlunar mission. The Earthrise picture is often credited with encouraging the environmental movement of the 1970s.

spc-apollo-13.why: The oxygen tank had been damaged before launch. It had once been dropped, and its heater switches were not rated for the launch pad's higher voltage, so wiring insulation was scorched during a ground test. When the crew stirred the tank's contents, a spark ignited it.
spc-apollo-13.impact: An investigation led to a redesigned oxygen tank, an extra tank and a backup battery on later flights, and Apollo 14 was delayed until 1971. NASA called the mission a successful failure. The improvised fixes, such as adapting air filters, are still cited as problem-solving under pressure.

spc-salyut-1.why: After losing the race to the Moon, the Soviet Union shifted its emphasis to long stays in Earth orbit. Salyut 1 was put together quickly using hardware from a military station project and Soyuz systems, partly in order to fly before the American Skylab.
spc-salyut-1.impact: The Soyuz was redesigned and for several years carried only two cosmonauts, in suits. Salyut 1 was deliberately brought down after about six months, but six more Salyut stations followed, giving the Soviet Union long experience of living in orbit that led on to Mir.

spc-apollo-soyuz.why: The flight grew out of détente. Nixon and Soviet premier Alexei Kosygin signed a space cooperation agreement in Moscow in 1972. Engineers had to design a shared docking system and an airlock, because the two spacecraft used different cabin atmospheres and pressures.
spc-apollo-soyuz.impact: It was the last Apollo flight, and no American flew in space again until the shuttle in 1981. Cooperation lapsed as relations worsened in the late 1970s, then resumed in the 1990s with shuttle visits to Mir, building on the contacts made between engineers.

spc-viking-1.why: Mariner 9 had mapped Mars from orbit in 1971 and found dry river channels, raising hopes that life might once have existed. Viking was NASA's costly follow-up, with two orbiters and two landers. The landing was planned for 4 July 1976 but delayed to find a smoother site.
spc-viking-1.impact: Viking measured the thin carbon dioxide atmosphere and the composition of the soil, and its orbiters mapped the planet in detail. With no clear sign of life, NASA sent no further landers for twenty years, until Mars Pathfinder in 1997.

spc-voyager-1.why: In the late 1970s the outer planets lined up in a way that occurs roughly every 175 years, letting a probe use each planet's gravity to reach the next. NASA scaled back a larger Grand Tour plan to two craft. Voyager 1 launched after Voyager 2 but on a faster path.
spc-voyager-1.impact: It discovered active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io and studied the thick atmosphere of Saturn's moon Titan, a detour that sent it out of the plane of the planets. The findings shaped later missions such as Galileo and Cassini. Its instruments now sample the space between the stars.

spc-shuttle-columbia.why: After Apollo, NASA wanted a cheaper, reusable way to reach orbit, and Nixon approved the shuttle in 1972. Development ran years late because of problems with the main engines and the heat-shield tiles. Unusually, the first flight carried a crew, with no unmanned test beforehand.
spc-shuttle-columbia.impact: The shuttle launched satellites, the Hubble telescope and most of the International Space Station. It never became cheap or routine, and two orbiters were lost with fourteen crew, Challenger in 1986 and Columbia itself in 2003. The fleet was retired in 2011.

spc-sally-ride.why: NASA's astronauts had all been men, mostly military pilots. For the shuttle it created the role of mission specialist for scientists and engineers, and its 1978 intake of 35 included six women and the first African American and Asian American astronauts.
spc-sally-ride.impact: Ride faced press questions about her sex that male colleagues never did, and became a role model for girls interested in science. Kathryn Sullivan made the first spacewalk by an American woman in 1984. Ride later founded a company promoting science education and died in 2012.

spc-challenger.why: Engineers at the booster maker Morton Thiokol had seen seal erosion on earlier flights and urged a delay because of the cold, but were overruled by managers. NASA was under pressure to keep to a busy launch schedule, and the flight had already been postponed several times.
spc-challenger.impact: The Rogers Commission, whose members included the physicist Richard Feynman, blamed flawed decision-making as well as the joint design. The boosters were redesigned, commercial satellites were moved to unmanned rockets, and the case became a standard study in engineering ethics and organisational failure.

spc-mir.why: The Salyut stations had at most two docking ports and could not be enlarged. Soviet designers gave Mir's core a node with several ports, so that laboratories could be added over time while crew and cargo ships still came and went. It built directly on Salyut 7.
spc-mir.impact: Mir outlived the Soviet Union, and a cash-short Russia opened it to paying foreign partners. From 1995 American shuttles docked there, teaching both sides how to work together. A fire and a collision with a cargo craft in 1997 gave hard lessons later applied to the International Space Station.

spc-hubble.why: Astronomers, notably Lyman Spitzer from the 1940s, had argued for a telescope above the blurring and filtering of the atmosphere. Congress funded it in 1977, with European participation. Launch slipped from 1983 because of technical delays and then the grounding of the shuttle after Challenger.
spc-hubble.impact: Hubble narrowed down the rate at which the universe expands, and so its age, and contributed to the discovery that the expansion is accelerating. Its deep field images showed thousands of very distant galaxies. Five shuttle servicing missions kept it working decades beyond its planned life.

spc-iss-zarya.why: The United States had planned its own station, Freedom, since 1984, but costs kept rising. After the Soviet collapse, Washington invited Russia to join in 1993, merging Freedom with Russia's planned Mir 2. The deal was also meant to keep Russian rocket engineers employed in peaceful work.
spc-iss-zarya.impact: The first resident crew arrived in November 2000 and the station has been continuously occupied since. It grew to roughly the size of a football pitch, with European, Japanese and Canadian contributions. After the shuttle retired in 2011, Russian Soyuz craft were the only crew transport until 2020.

spc-falcon-1.why: Elon Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 with money from the sale of PayPal, after concluding that existing rockets were too expensive. The company built its own engines to cut costs. The earlier launches failed through a fuel leak, an early engine shutdown and a collision between stages.
spc-falcon-1.impact: Falcon 1 flew only once more before SpaceX moved to the larger Falcon 9, which first launched in 2010. Reusable Falcon 9 boosters, first landed in 2015, sharply lowered launch prices. The company began carrying NASA astronauts to the space station in 2020.

spc-curiosity.why: The earlier rovers Spirit and Opportunity had found evidence that liquid water once existed on Mars. NASA wanted a larger mobile laboratory to test whether conditions were ever suitable for microbes. Gale Crater was chosen for its central mountain of layered rock, which records a long span of Martian history.
spc-curiosity.impact: The rover found rounded pebbles from an ancient stream bed and mudstones laid down in a lake, and it detected organic molecules and changing levels of methane. The sky crane method was used again to land the Perseverance rover in 2021.

spc-new-horizons-pluto.why: Pluto was the only one of the nine classical planets never visited by a spacecraft. Several earlier mission proposals were cancelled before NASA approved New Horizons in 2001. Scientists wanted to arrive before Pluto moved farther from the Sun, when its thin atmosphere might freeze onto the surface.
spc-new-horizons-pluto.impact: Pluto proved geologically active, with few craters on its icy plains, which surprised researchers who expected a dead world. Its moon Charon showed canyons and a dark polar cap. In 2019 the probe flew past Arrokoth, a small Kuiper belt object and the most distant body yet visited.

spc-black-hole-image.why: No single telescope is sharp enough to resolve a black hole's shadow. The technique of linking distant radio dishes had been refined for decades, and by 2017 enough observatories working at short wavelengths, including ALMA in Chile, existed to form an Earth-sized instrument. Atomic clocks kept their recordings synchronised.
spc-black-hole-image.impact: The image gave direct visual evidence for black holes, which had previously been inferred from their effects on nearby stars and gas. In 2022 the same collaboration released a picture of Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy.

spc-jwst.why: Astronomers began planning a successor to Hubble in the 1990s. To see the first galaxies, whose light has been stretched into the infrared by the expansion of the universe, it needed a very large mirror kept extremely cold, hence the folding design and the sunshield the size of a tennis court.
spc-jwst.impact: Webb has found galaxies from the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang, some brighter and more developed than models predicted. It has also analysed the atmospheres of planets orbiting other stars. A precise launch left enough fuel for well over ten years of operation.

spc-artemis-1.why: After the shuttle retired, Congress in 2010 directed NASA to build a heavy rocket using shuttle engines and boosters. The Artemis programme, named in 2019, set the goal of returning astronauts to the Moon. Technical problems, hydrogen leaks and a hurricane delayed the first launch repeatedly.
spc-artemis-1.impact: Orion's heat shield wore away more unevenly than predicted during re-entry, which prompted a long investigation and changes to later flight plans. The mission also tested the European-built service module. It cleared the way for Artemis II, a crewed flight around the Moon.
